pages.title: Introduction to Structures
pages.content:
In C++, structures are user-defined data types that allow you to group together different variables under a single name. 

Here's how you can define and use structures in C++:
- We define a structure named MyStruct using the `struct` keyword. Inside the structure, we declare three members: an int variable x, a double variable y, and a char variable c.
- In the main function, we declare a variable myObject of type MyStruct. This creates an instance of the structure.
- We access and initialize the structure members using the dot (.) operator. For example, myObject.x refers to the x member of the myObject structure.

Remember that structures in C++ can also have member functions, but they are limited in functionality compared to classes. It's generally recommended to use classes for more complex data structures that require inheritance, encapsulation and abstraction, while using structs for simpler data containers.

questions.question: What is the default access specifier for members of a C++ `struct`?
questions.explanation: In C++, struct members default to public visibility, whereas class members default to private.

questions.question: What is a "scoped enumeration" (`enum class`) in modern C++?
options: An enum that can only hold strings
A strongly typed enum whose enumerators are scoped inside the enum and do not implicitly convert to int
An enum that can be resized
questions.explanation: enum class enforces strong typing and scoping (Color::Red), preventing implicit integer conversion bugs.

questions.question: What C++17 library type in `<variant>` provides a type-safe, exception-safe alternative to C unions?
questions.explanation: std::variant is a type-safe tagged union holding one of several specified types, knowing its active type at all times.

questions.question: Can a C++ `struct` have constructors and member functions?
options: No, only classes can have constructors
Yes, structs in C++ can have constructors, destructors, and methods
questions.explanation: In C++, structs are full classes with default public visibility, supporting constructors and member functions.

questions.question: What is "default member initialization" introduced in C++11?
options: Assigning default values directly in the struct definition (e.g. `int count = 0;`)
questions.explanation: C++11 allows in-class member initializers (`int x = 0;`), which are applied automatically across all constructors.

questions.question: What is the size of a C++ `union` containing `int` (4B) and `double` (8B)?
questions.explanation: The size of a union is dictated by its largest member, which is double (8 bytes).

questions.question: Can underlying storage types be specified for an `enum class` (e.g. `enum class Flag : uint8_t`)?
options: Yes, any integral type can be specified to control byte size
questions.explanation: C++11 allows specifying explicit underlying types for enums (e.g. : uint8_t) to minimize memory usage.

questions.question: What C++17 type in `<optional>` represents a value that may or may not be present without pointer overhead?
questions.explanation: std::optional<T> manages an optional value that may be empty (`std::nullopt`), avoiding null pointer bugs.

questions.question: What is aggregate initialization in C++?
options: Initializing structs/classes that have no user-declared constructors using braces `{arg1, arg2}`
questions.explanation: Aggregate initialization allows initializing simple structs directly member-by-member using `{val1, val2}`.

questions.question: What does `sizeof` on an empty struct `struct Empty {};` return in C++?
options: 1 byte (so different objects have unique memory addresses)
questions.explanation: To ensure distinct objects have distinct memory addresses, the C++ standard requires empty classes/structs to have sizeof at least 1.
